entry: Activities involving physical intimacy, contact with the genitals or erogenous zones, and erotic stimulation. Sexual acts range from solitary activities such as [[Masturbation|masturbation]] to acts with one or more partners, including [[Sexual intercourse|sexual intercourse]], [[Oral sex|oral sex]] and non-penetrative sex. Sexual activity usually produces [[Sexual arousal|sexual arousal]] and physiological changes, and conduct such as [[Foreplay|foreplay]] is intended to arouse a partner's interest. Human sexual activity has sociological, cognitive, emotional, behavioral and biological aspects. In some cultures it is considered acceptable only within [[Marriage|marriage]], while premarital and extramarital sex are taboo. [[Sexual assault]] and sexual activity with a person below the age of consent are criminal offenses in most jurisdictions. Activity under force or duress is considered [[Rape|rape]] or another form of sexual assault.

Internal framework of the body. Around 270 bones are present at birth, and some fuse together, leaving about 206 by adulthood, not counting accessory bones. Bone mass makes up about 14% of total body weight, or 10–11 kg in an average person, and peaks between the ages of 25 and 30. The axial skeleton, formed by the [[Spinal column|spinal column]], rib cage, [[Skull|skull]] and associated bones, maintains upright posture; the appendicular skeleton, formed by the shoulder and pelvic girdles and the limbs, makes locomotion possible. The skeleton performs six major functions: support, movement, protection, production of blood cells, storage of minerals and endocrine regulation. Blood cells develop in bone marrow, mainly in the long bones in children and in the pelvis, cranium, vertebrae and sternum in adults. The bone matrix stores [[Calcium|calcium]]. The female pelvis is shaped to facilitate [[Childbirth|childbirth]].

Unlawful recruitment, transport or buying of people through force, fraud or coercion for exploitation. Exploitation may include forced labor, [[Slavery|sexual slavery]] or other forms of commercial sexual exploitation. Trafficking is a form of modern slavery, a crime against humanity and a serious violation of [[Human rights|human rights]]. Unlike people smuggling, which involves the consent of the person smuggled, trafficking involves exploitation without consent. Trafficking can occur within a single country or across national borders. International agreements, such as the [[United Nations|UN]] Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, condemn it, but legal protections and enforcement vary significantly across countries. Millions of women, men and children are estimated to be victims. A 2024 report by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime found that children made up 38% of detected victims from 2020 to 2023, including 22% girls and 16% boys.

Sound made by the vocal tract, including speech, singing, laughing, crying and screaming. The [[Lung|lungs]] supply airflow, and the vocal folds (vocal cords) vibrate to create audible pulses. The larynx muscles adjust the folds' length and tension to set pitch, and the articulators of the vocal tract, including the [[Tongue|tongue]], palate, cheeks and lips, filter the sound. Adult male vocal folds are between 17 mm and 25 mm long, and female folds between 12.5 mm and 17.5 mm. Men generally have a larger vocal tract, which gives a lower timbre. The tone can be modulated to suggest emotions such as [[Anger|anger]], surprise, [[Fear|fear]], [[Happiness|happiness]] or [[Sadness|sadness]], and the voice can reveal the age and sex of the speaker. Singers use it as an instrument, with categories such as bass, baritone and tenor for men and contralto, mezzo-soprano and soprano for women.

Philosophical stance centered on the agency and potential of human beings, seen as the starting point for moral and philosophical inquiry. The meaning of the term has changed as successive movements claimed it. Italian scholars inspired by Greek classical scholarship gave rise to [[Renaissance]] humanism, and during the [[Age of Enlightenment]], humanistic values were reinforced by advances in science and technology. In the early 21st century the term generally denotes a focus on [[Well-being|well-being]], human freedom and progress, and the equal and inherent dignity of all human beings. Humanists tend to advocate human rights, free speech, progressive policies and democracy. Contemporary humanism is generally [[Theism|non-theistic]], relying on science and reason rather than divine revelation. Organized humanist movements since the 20th century are mostly non-religious and aligned with [[Secularism|secularism]]. The word derives from the Latin *humanitas*, used by [[Cicero]] for values related to liberal education.

Psychological perspective of the early- to mid-20th century, developed as a response to psychoanalysis and [[Behaviorism|behaviorism]]. Otto Rank and [[Carl Rogers]] centered the individual in therapy, and [[Abraham Maslow]] built on their work to establish a "third force" in psychology in the 1950s. Maslow criticized [[Sigmund Freud|Freud]]'s theory as deterministic, and argued that both Freud and [[B. F. Skinner|Skinner]] focused on people with mental conflicts rather than on all individuals. Humanistic psychology seeks to understand people holistically, as wholes greater than the sums of their parts, and it stresses intentionality. It treats spiritual aspiration as an integral part of the psyche, and is linked to transpersonal psychology. Humanistic therapy encourages self-awareness so that clients can move from one set of reactions to a healthier one. Its principal US organizations are the Association for Humanistic Psychology and the Society for Humanistic Psychology.

Beliefs and practices centered on the value of human life, aimed at reducing suffering through assistance to others. Unlike charity and philanthropy, which apply to both domestic and international projects, humanitarianism tends to involve helping populations affected by international emergencies such as wars and disasters. It overlaps with [[Human rights|human rights]] advocacy, development assistance and domestic philanthropy. Its motivations range between [[Altruism|altruism]] and market affinity, and its links to religious belief, [[Imperialism|imperialism]], neo-colonialism and [[Social control|social control]] are also examined. Scholars date global humanitarian impulses to the 19th century. The founding of the [[International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement]] in 1863 marks a key juncture. In the mid-19th century, [[Florence Nightingale]] and [[Henry Dunant]] were central to emergency response, and Dunant's work led to the founding of the Red Cross. Michael Barnett distinguishes ages of "imperial humanitarianism" (late 19th century to 1945), "neo-humanitarianism" (1945–1989) and "liberal humanitarianism" (post-1990).

Academic disciplines studying human society and culture, using mainly critical, speculative or interpretive methods. The humanities include [[Philosophy|philosophy]], religion, [[History|history]], language arts such as [[Literature|literature]] and [[Rhetoric|rhetoric]], the performing arts and the visual arts. During the [[Renaissance]], the term referred to the study of classical literature and language, as opposed to divinity. The Latin phrase *studia humanitatis* covered grammar, literature, rhetoric, history and moral philosophy. Historically the humanities have been distinguished from the [[Social science|social sciences]] by their methods and objectives. The humanities take an idiographic approach that focuses on the unique and context-specific, while the social sciences seek general laws through empirical and quantitative analysis, a distinction first conceptualized by Wilhelm Windelband. The distinction is not absolute, since some social scientists use narrative inquiry and historical methods. Proponents argue the humanities foster self-reflection, civic responsibility and cultural continuity.

Second [[Mughal Empire|Mughal]] emperor (r. 1530–1540, 1555–1556). He succeeded his father, [[Babur]], on December 26, 1530, as ruler of the Mughal territories in the Indian subcontinent, but was inexperienced when he came to power at 22. His half-brother Kamran Mirza inherited [[Kabul]] and [[Kandahar]], and the two became bitter rivals. Early in his reign he lost the empire to [[Sher Shah Suri]] and fled to Persia; he regained it 15 years later with Safavid aid. His return from Persia was accompanied by a large retinue of Persian noblemen, signaling an important change in court culture. The dynasty's Central Asian origins were largely overshadowed by [[Persian art]], architecture, language and literature. Thousands of Persian manuscripts from his time survive in India. He expanded the empire quickly after returning to power, leaving a substantial legacy for his son, [[Akbar]]. At his death, the empire spanned almost one million square kilometers.

Public research university in the Mitte borough of [[Berlin]], Germany. Established by Frederick William III of Prussia in 1809 on the initiative of Wilhelm von Humboldt, it opened in 1810. It was renamed in 1949 in honor of Alexander and Wilhelm von Humboldt. It was generally regarded as the world's preeminent university for the natural sciences in the 19th and early 20th centuries and is linked to major breakthroughs in physics by professors such as [[Albert Einstein]]. Its faculty and alumni include 57 [[Nobel Prize]] laureates, the most of any German university. It has nine faculties and around 35,000 students, and its main campus is on Unter den Linden in central Berlin. During the [[Cold War]] it was in East Berlin, and it was de facto split in two when the Free University of Berlin opened in West Berlin.

Temperate climate type with long, hot summers and cool to mild winters. Normally found on the southeast side of continents, generally between latitudes 25° and 40°, it lies poleward of tropical climates. Under the [[Köppen climate classification|Köppen]] system, Cfa and Cwa climates are described as humid subtropical or warm temperate, though Köppen himself never used the term. Under the Trewartha system, climates are humid subtropical when they have at least 8 months with a mean temperature above 10 °C (50 °F). Rainfall often peaks in summer, and winters are normally mild.

Concentration of [[Water vapor|water vapor]] in the air, indicating the likelihood of [[Precipitation|precipitation]], [[Dew|dew]] or [[Fog|fog]]. Humidity depends on temperature and pressure. The same amount of water vapor gives a higher relative humidity in cool air than in warm air, and the [[Dew point|dew point]] is the temperature at which air reaches saturation. Absolute humidity is the mass of water vapor per volume of air, in grams per cubic meter. Relative humidity, often expressed as a percentage, indicates the present amount relative to the maximum at the same temperature. Specific humidity is the ratio of water vapor mass to total moist air mass. High humidity impairs heat exchange for animals that rely on sweating, because it reduces the rate of [[Evaporation|evaporation]] from skin surfaces; a heat index table or a humidex can estimate the effect.

Family of small birds native to the Americas, comprising Trochilidae. The family has around 375 species in 113 genera, from [[Alaska]] to [[Tierra del Fuego]], with most species in Central and South America. Hummingbirds are the smallest mature birds, measuring 7.5–13 cm (3–5 in) long. The bee hummingbird weighs less than 2.0 g, and the giant hummingbird, at 23 cm (9 in), is the largest. Male plumage shows the widest color diversity of any birds. Their wings beat so fast that they produce a humming sound, and they have the highest mass-specific metabolic rate of any homeothermic animal. Hummingbirds feed mainly on flower nectar, and all species also consume small [[Insect|insects]]. Most do not migrate, but the rufous hummingbird travels about 3,900 miles (6,300 km) twice a year between Alaska and [[Mexico]]. The family split from its sister group, the [[Swift (bird)|swifts]], around 42 million years ago.

[[Levant|Levantine]] dip of mashed [[Chickpea|chickpeas]] blended with tahini, lemon juice and garlic. The name is Arabic for "chickpeas", and the dish is usually eaten as a dip with pita bread. The earliest mention is in a 13th-century cookbook attributed to the historian Ibn al-Adim of [[Aleppo]], in present-day [[Syria]]. In the West it is produced industrially and eaten as a snack or appetizer with crackers or vegetables.

System of medicine adopted by Ancient Greek and Roman physicians, based on four bodily fluids. Its four humors were blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, and [[Hippocrates]] is usually credited with applying the idea to medicine. Illness was seen as an extreme excess or deficiency of a humor, and health as their correct proportion. [[Galen]] systematized the theory. It began to fall out of favor in the 17th century and was definitively disproved with the discovery of microbes.

Baleen whale species, the only member of the genus Megaptera. Adults range from 14–17 m (46–56 ft) in length and weigh up to 40 metric tons. The humpback is known for breaching. Males produce a complex song that typically lasts from 4 to 33 minutes. Humpbacks migrate between feeding areas toward the poles and breeding areas near the equator, and they feed mostly on [[Krill|krill]] and small fish, often using bubbles to catch prey. [[Orca|Orcas]] are the main natural predators of humpbacks. Like other large whales, the humpback was a target of the [[Whaling|whaling industry]] and was hunted to the brink of extinction, its population falling to around 5,000 by the 1960s. Numbers have partially recovered to some 135,000 animals, but entanglement in fishing gear, collisions with ships and noise pollution continue to affect the species.

American actor, known for gangster and detective roles in film noir. Nicknamed Bogie, he rose to stardom in 1941 with leading roles in *High Sierra* and *The Maltese Falcon*. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *The African Queen* (1951) and was Oscar-nominated for *Casablanca* (1942) and *The Caine Mutiny* (1954). He acted opposite [[Lauren Bacall]] in several films, including *To Have and Have Not* (1944) and *The Big Sleep* (1946), and was married to her from 1945 until his death. He was honored with a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1960, and the American Film Institute named him the greatest male star of classic American cinema in 1999. Four of his films were named in the AFI's Top 100 films of all time.

British chemist and inventor of the Davy lamp and an early form of arc lamp. Using electricity, he isolated [[Potassium|potassium]] and [[Sodium|sodium]] in 1807 and [[Calcium|calcium]], strontium, barium, magnesium and boron the following year. He also discovered the elemental nature of [[Chlorine|chlorine]] and iodine and invented the new field of [[Electrochemistry|electrochemistry]]. In 1799 he experimented with [[Nitrous oxide|nitrous oxide]], nicknamed it "laughing gas", and wrote about its potential as an anesthetic to relieve pain during surgery. He was a baronet and president of the Royal Society, and a founder member of the Geological Society of London. Berzelius called his 1806 Bakerian Lecture "one of the best memoirs which has ever enriched the theory of chemistry." He also wrote over 160 manuscript poems, most of which were not published.

Inland province in Central China, in the middle reaches of the [[Yangtze]] watershed. Its capital and largest city is [[Changsha]], on the Xiang River. With just over 66 million people as of 2020 in an area of about 210,000 sq km (81,000 sq mi), it is China's 7th-most populous province. The name means "south of the lake," referring to Dongting Lake, and Hunan was the birthplace of [[Mao Zedong]], who became chairman of the Chinese Communist Party and founding father of the People's Republic of China. Most residents are [[Han Chinese]], and the province also has Tujia and Miao minorities. [[UNESCO]] inscribed Wulingyuan as a World Heritage Site in 1992. The province is the seat of the Yuelu Academy, later Hunan University, one of the four major academies over the last 1,000 years in ancient China.

1815 period of the [[Napoleonic Wars]], from [[Napoleon]]'s return from exile on Elba to the second restoration of [[Louis XVIII]]. It lasted 110 days, from March 20 to July 8, 1815, and included the Waterloo campaign and the War of the Seventh Coalition. The Congress of Vienna declared Napoleon an outlaw, and four Great Powers pledged 150,000 men each to end his rule. Napoleon was defeated at the [[Battle of Waterloo]], after which he was exiled to [[Saint Helena]], where he died.

Series of medieval conflicts between England and France, 1337–1453. It emerged from feudal disputes over the Duchy of Aquitaine and was triggered by a claim to the French throne made by [[Edward III]] of England. The periodization of the war typically charts it as taking place over 116 years, but it was intermittent, interrupted by truces and by events such as the [[Black Death]]. It is commonly divided into the Edwardian War (1337–1360), the Caroline War (1369–1389) and the Lancastrian War (1415–1453). Five generations of kings from two rival dynasties fought for the French throne. Both sides produced innovations in military technology and tactics, including professional standing armies and [[Artillery|artillery]]. [[Chivalry]] reached its height during the conflict and then declined. Ultimately the House of Valois retained control of the [[Kingdom of France]], and the French and English monarchies remained separate.

Attempted countrywide uprising against Hungary's communist government and Soviet domination. It began on October 23, 1956, in [[Budapest]], when university students appealed to the public to join them in protest against the government of Mátyás Rákosi. After a delegation of students who had entered the Hungarian radio building was detained, ÁVH police fatally shot several students outside, and revolutionaries broke into the building. Revolutionary militias formed, and the new government of [[Imre Nagy]] disbanded the ÁVH and declared Hungary's withdrawal from the [[Warsaw Pact]]. The [[Soviet Union]] repressed the revolution from November 4, and fighting continued until November 10. Repression killed 2,000 Hungarians and 700 Soviet soldiers, and about 200,000 Hungarians sought refuge abroad, mostly in [[Austria]].

Ugric language of the [[Uralic languages|Uralic]] family, official in [[Hungary]] and one of the 24 official languages of the [[European Union]]. Also called Magyar, it has 14 million speakers, the most of any Uralic language. Hungarian communities live in southern [[Slovakia]], western [[Ukraine]], [[Transylvania]] in Romania, Vojvodina in Serbia, and parts of Croatia, Slovenia and Austria, as well as North America and [[Israel]]. Hungarian belongs to the Ugric branch with Mansi and Khanty, though that grouping is debated. Historically it was written in the Old Hungarian script, an alphabetic system believed to derive from the Old Turkic script. Its vocabulary contains loanwords from Turkic, Slavic and German sources, reflecting contact after the Hungarians settled in the Carpathian Basin.

Landlocked country in [[Central Europe]], spanning much of the Carpathian Basin. It has a population of over 9.5 million, mostly ethnic Hungarians. [[Budapest]] is the capital. Statehood began in the late ninth century, and in 1000 it became a Christian kingdom under King Stephen I. After defeat by the [[Ottoman Empire]] at the Battle of Mohács in 1526, the kingdom was split into three regions for over 150 years. Uprisings against the Habsburgs led to the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy in the Compromise of 1867. The 1920 Treaty of Trianon set modern borders and cost Hungary 71% of its historical territory. After World War II, the Hungarian People's Republic was established in 1949 as a satellite state within the [[Warsaw Pact]], and the [[Hungarian Revolution of 1956|1956 uprising]] failed. During the Revolutions of 1989 it became a democratic parliamentary republic, joining the [[European Union]] in 2004 and the [[Schengen Area]] in 2007.

Sustained inability to consume enough food to meet basic nutritional needs. Hunger differs from appetite, the typical desire for food. Its most severe form is [[Famine|famine]], declared when people start dying of starvation. By 2015, the threat of extreme hunger had receded for a large portion of the world's population, but the 2023 report of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) found the trend had reversed from about 2017. Hunger rose during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] in 2020 and 2021, and recovered in 2022. In 2023, 8.2% of the global population experienced hunger, down from 8.5% in 2022 and 8.7% in 2021. FAO identified climate, conflict and economic slowdowns as three causes of the recent increase, and much of the rise since 2017 occurred in [[Africa]] and [[South America]]. The [[United Nations|UN]] coordinates much of the global hunger relief effort, aiming at SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) by 2030.
